narration: Rome flushed toilets with water that someone had already bathed in. That sounds backwards. But used bathwater had another job: carry waste away. Follow the route beneath the city, and a clever machine reveals a troubling gap. The Romans recycled water from public baths as part of the flow that flushed latrines. A stream beneath the seats carried waste onward. Public toilets could have long benches with rows of openings, offering little privacy. The main drain had begun as an open channel to drain low-lying ground. Covering it came later, as drainage evolved. The engineering worked at the scale of channels, buildings, and streets. But what happened inside a home that never joined the network? Most dwellings were not connected to street drains or sewers. Some wealthy households had outlets beneath their latrines, while poorer residents used pots they were supposed to empty into the sewer, or visited public toilets. Access was uneven. Underground drainage could move water without connecting every household above it. And the famous main drain had started with another problem: draining low-lying land around the Forum. Its channels later carried rainwater, debris, and waste toward the Tiber River. Water from the baths was reused, but reuse was not the same as purification. Despite sewers, baths, and public latrines, disease remained widespread. That is the tension hidden beneath Rome: an impressive route for moving waste, without a universal solution to sanitation. The drains show ingenuity. The unconnected homes show the limit. Following the water tells both stories.
